title: Cutting Online Misinformation May Not Change Beliefs
paragraphs: Many people believe that misinformation on social media shapes what people think, and that reducing it would change people's beliefs. However, a large new study suggests that the situation may be more complicated.

The study was published in the journal Science Advances in 2026. It was carried out by a team of academic researchers, including Brendan Nyhan of Dartmouth College and Olivier Bergeron-Boutin of the University of California, Berkeley, together with researchers from Meta, the company that owns Facebook and Instagram. Importantly, the academic researchers kept final control over the analysis and did not receive payment from Meta.

The experiment took place around the time of the 2020 US presidential election and lasted about three months. It involved 15,928 adults who agreed to take part, including many people who regularly saw content from untrustworthy sources. For half of the participants, the amount of untrustworthy content shown in their feeds was reduced. On Facebook, its share fell from 1.8% to 0.5%, and on Instagram, it fell from 2.5% to 0.8%. In both cases, this was a reduction of around 70%. The researchers then measured the participants' opinions using surveys.

Surprisingly, reducing misinformation had almost no measurable effect. It did not change people's beliefs about false claims, their trust in mainstream media or their political attitudes. Even people who had previously consumed large amounts of untrustworthy content did not change their views. According to Bergeron-Boutin, the intervention worked as intended, but the changes in attitudes were much smaller than some people had expected.
The researchers also found that most users saw relatively little untrustworthy content to begin with. Most of it was seen by a minority of users.

However, experts warn against concluding that misinformation is harmless. The study only covered one election, on two platforms that have changed since 2020, and three months may be too short to measure effects that develop over years. In addition, other researchers pointed out that exposure to problematic content could increase significantly if platforms stopped removing it. Since Meta ended its fact-checking program in the United States in January 2025, the experiment cannot be repeated in the same way.
Other recent studies suggest that correcting misinformation after people see it can reduce its influence.
